groups.title: Edge and internal-plane identity-header trust boundary
groups.problem: A caller can tell the platform who they are simply by saying so in a request header, and the platform believes it. Someone who can reach the service can present themselves as another customer's administrator and read or change that customer's data, and the usage is billed to whoever they claimed to be. Operators have no way to tell a genuine request from a claimed one after the fact.
groups.fix_in_one_line: Stop treating caller-supplied identity headers as identity: strip them at the edge and resolve identity server-side on every path that currently reads them.
groups.goal: Make caller-supplied identity headers non-authoritative everywhere, so identity is always resolved from a verified session rather than read out of a request the caller controls.
groups.motivation: These four findings are one defect with four reachable entry points: the edge does not remove the headers, and three request paths read them as if it had. Fixing them separately would leave whichever path is fixed last as a complete bypass of the other three, so they are one piece of work.
groups.who_benefits: every tenant on the shared gateway — this class of gap is what allows one tenant to act as another
groups.who_is_impacted: security (the trust boundary itself), billing (spend attribution follows the claimed identity), support (account-takeover reports), ops (the edge configuration changes)

risks.bug_class: A path is missed and still reads the header
risks.blast_radius: That path remains a full identity bypass; the other three fixes buy nothing

risks.bug_class: The edge strips a header a legitimate internal caller needs
risks.blast_radius: Internal callers fail closed — a visible outage rather than a silent bypass, which is the preferred direction

risks.bug_class: Server-side resolution is added but the old read is left as a fallback
risks.blast_radius: The bypass survives behind a code path that looks fixed on review

groups.cost_footprint: code plus one edge configuration change. No new tables, no new compute, nothing unbounded.
groups.approach: Remove the identity headers at the edge so they cannot arrive, then make each request path resolve identity from the verified session instead of reading the header. Both halves are required: the edge change alone leaves any non-edge route exposed, and the route change alone leaves the header arriving.
groups.deployment: Gateway code ships to dev on merge via `gateway-deploy.yml`. The edge configuration change is Terraform and requires a manual `gateway-infra-apply.yml` dispatch — it will NOT apply on merge. No agent-runtime image rebuild. Rollback: revert the PR for the code half; re-apply the previous policy for the edge half.
groups.validation: Unit tests proving each affected path ignores the header and resolves identity from the session; a test proving the header is absent by the time a route handler runs. Smoke: a request carrying a forged identity header resolves to the authenticated caller, not the claimed one. Regression: existing authenticated flows and internal-plane routing keep working.

groups.title: Sign-in gate and session-token transport
groups.problem: The sign-in path lets people in who were never meant to have access, and once they are in, the token that proves who they are is handed to the browser in a place other code on the page can read. Together that means an unintended account can be created and its session can then be lifted by anything running in the page.
groups.fix_in_one_line: Make the sign-in gate enforce its configured policy, and move the session token to a transport the page cannot read.
groups.goal: Ensure sign-in admits only principals the configured policy allows, and that the resulting session credential is not readable by page-level code.
groups.motivation: The two findings compound: a weak gate decides who gets a session, and a readable session decides how far that session travels. Fixing one without the other leaves either unintended accounts with safe sessions or intended accounts with liftable ones.
groups.who_benefits: every user of the hosted sign-in flow, and operators who rely on the access policy meaning what it says
groups.who_is_impacted: security (authentication boundary), support (unexpected-account reports), the frontend sign-in flow

risks.bug_class: The gate is tightened without the configuration that admits legitimate users
risks.blast_radius: Total sign-in outage — every login fails, including operators'

risks.bug_class: Transport changed on the write side only
risks.blast_radius: Sessions are issued in a form the client cannot read; users appear signed out immediately after signing in

groups.cost_footprint: code only, across the broker and the frontend sign-in path. No new resources.
groups.approach: Make the gate fail closed when its policy and its permissive flag disagree, and change the session credential's transport so page-level code cannot read it. Ship both halves together, and make sure the configuration the tightened gate needs lands with, not after, the code that enforces it.
groups.deployment: Broker code publishes on merge; the environment variable the tightened gate reads lands only via a manual `gateway-infra-apply.yml`. Those two must not be separated — the gap between them is a login outage, which is on record. Frontend ships via the gateway frontend build. Rollback: restore the previous gate value on the live function first, then revert.
groups.validation: Unit tests for each gate decision including the fail-closed case; a test proving the session credential is not exposed to page-level code. Smoke: sign in end to end, then confirm the credential is unreadable from the page. Regression: existing sessions keep working across the change.

groups.title: Server-side role resolution instead of a default-admin fallback
groups.problem: Anyone who signs in is treated as an administrator of their organisation, because the platform has no real record of who is one. Every permission check that asks 'is this an admin?' therefore answers yes, so the checks read as protection while granting nothing of the kind.
groups.fix_in_one_line: Resolve each principal's role from the stored role record instead of defaulting every authenticated caller to administrator.
groups.goal: Give role resolution a real source of truth so authorization checks distinguish an administrator from an ordinary member.
groups.motivation: This is foundational rather than urgent-in-isolation: the per-endpoint gates in the other work items only become least-privilege once the default authority they consult is correct. Filed on its own because its fix surface is the authority model, not any one endpoint.
groups.who_benefits: every tenant with more than one member, and every endpoint whose gate currently resolves to a permanent yes
groups.who_is_impacted: security (the authority model), the admin UI, ops (existing members' effective roles change)

risks.bug_class: Existing members have no stored role and default to none
risks.blast_radius: Legitimate administrators lose access — visible and reversible, but disruptive

risks.bug_class: The fallback is narrowed but not removed
risks.blast_radius: Some paths keep the default-admin behaviour and the gates built on them stay vacuous

groups.cost_footprint: code plus reads against the existing role store. No new table.
groups.approach: Replace the default-admin fallback with a lookup against the stored role record, and decide explicitly what an absent record means. Absent must not mean administrator; a migration or a seeding step is needed for existing members so the tightening does not lock them out.
groups.deployment: Gateway code ships to dev on merge. If a data migration is needed for existing members it runs via the gateway migration workflow, not automatically on merge — state which. No infra apply. Rollback: revert the PR; the change is read-side only if no migration ships with it.
groups.validation: Unit tests for each role a principal can resolve to, including the absent-record case. Smoke: a non-administrator member is refused an administrator-only endpoint. Regression: administrators keep their access, and the admin UI still renders for them.

groups.title: Missing and broken authorization gates on tenant endpoints
groups.problem: Several endpoints accept an identifier from the caller and return or modify whatever it points at without checking that the caller is entitled to it. A customer can therefore reach another customer's records by changing a number in a request, and one administrative route can be called with no entitlement check at all.
groups.fix_in_one_line: Add a tenant-scope check to every one of these endpoints so an object identifier alone never grants access to it.
groups.goal: Ensure each of these endpoints authorizes the caller against the object it is being asked to act on, rather than trusting the identifier supplied.
groups.motivation: The three findings are the same missing check on three routes and share one fix pattern, so grouping them means the pattern is decided once and applied consistently instead of three times with three shapes.
groups.who_benefits: every tenant whose records are reachable through these routes
groups.who_is_impacted: security (tenant isolation), billing (one of the routes exposes spend data), support (cross-tenant data-access reports)

risks.bug_class: The check is added to two routes and missed on the third
risks.blast_radius: The unfixed route remains a complete cross-tenant read path, and the fix reads as complete

risks.bug_class: The check is scoped to the wrong attribute
risks.blast_radius: Access is refused for legitimate callers, or still granted across tenants — the latter is silent

groups.cost_footprint: code only, plus one additional scope read per request on the affected routes. No new resources.
groups.approach: Apply the existing tenant-scope check pattern to each route rather than inventing a new one, so all three read the same way in review. Enumerate every route in the affected modules that takes a caller-supplied identifier, so the fix covers the class and not only the three reported instances.
groups.deployment: Gateway code ships to dev on merge via `gateway-deploy.yml`. No Terraform apply, no image rebuild, no frontend build. Rollback: revert the PR — the change is code-only.
groups.validation: Per route: a test proving a caller from another tenant is refused, and a test proving the owning tenant still succeeds. Smoke: request another tenant's object on each route and confirm a refusal. Regression: existing same-tenant callers of all three routes keep working.

groups.title: Privileged write stores reachable without a privileged gate
groups.problem: Two stores that should only ever be written by a privileged operator can be written by an ordinary authenticated caller. One of them is where credentials live, so an unprivileged user can add or replace entries that other parts of the platform then trust and act on.
groups.fix_in_one_line: Put a privileged-operator gate in front of both write stores so an ordinary authenticated caller cannot write to either.
groups.goal: Restrict writes to these two stores to privileged operators, so nothing an ordinary caller can do changes what the rest of the platform trusts.
groups.motivation: Both are the same defect — a privileged write surface with an ordinary-caller gate — and both are consumed by other components that assume their contents are trustworthy. One fix pattern, applied to two stores, reviewed together.
groups.who_benefits: every tenant, and every component that reads these stores expecting operator-authored content
groups.who_is_impacted: security (credential-plane integrity), ops (the registry), support (tampering reports)

risks.bug_class: The gate is added to the route but not to the service the route calls
risks.blast_radius: Any other caller of that service keeps the unguarded write path

risks.bug_class: The gate resolves against the default-admin authority model
risks.blast_radius: The gate passes for every authenticated caller and protects nothing until the role-resolution work item lands

groups.approach: Gate both write paths at the service layer rather than only at the route, so every caller of the service inherits the check. Note the dependency on real role resolution: until roles resolve correctly, these gates are only as strong as the authority they consult.
groups.deployment: Gateway code ships to dev on merge via `gateway-deploy.yml`. No Terraform apply, no image rebuild. Rollback: revert the PR — code-only. Note the ordering dependency on the role-resolution work item; landing this first is safe but its effect is partial until that one lands.
groups.validation: Unit tests proving an ordinary authenticated caller is refused each write and a privileged operator is allowed, asserted at the service layer so route-only coverage cannot pass vacuously. Smoke: attempt each write as an ordinary caller and confirm a refusal. Regression: operator-driven writes to both stores keep working.
